summary: Describes a way to encapsulate IPX datagrams within UDP packets so that IPX traffic can travel across an IP internet. It began on the standards track but is now historic.

eli5.summary: Some computers speak a Novell language. This puts their messages inside Internet envelopes so they can cross the Internet.

questions: how to tunnel ipx over ip
subtitle: Carrying Novell IPX datagrams through IP networks using UDP.

tldr.problem: IPX networks (used by Novell NetWare) cannot natively cross IP internets, trapping IPX traffic within isolated networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes how to encapsulate IPX datagrams inside UDP packets, allowing IPX traffic to traverse IP networks. Each IPX packet becomes the payload of a UDP packet with the source and destination ports set to 213. Broadcasts are simulated by sending separate unicast packets to each peer in a configured list.
tldr.outcome: This approach allowed some interoperability between Novell and IP networks during the 1990s, but is now historic as both technologies have been superseded.

today: RFC 1234 is Historic. Both IPX and this tunneling approach have been superseded by modern IP-based networking. The RFC is preserved as a historical reference to an important interoperability solution of the NetWare era.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: IPX (Internet Packet eXchange) is the network protocol used by Novell's NetWare. Functionally, it is equivalent to the Internet Datagram Protocol from the Xerox Network Systems suite. However, IPX networks cannot natively cross IP internets. This RFC describes a way to encapsulate IPX datagrams within UDP packets so that IPX traffic can travel across IP networks. This allows an IPX implementation to view an IP internet as a single IPX network, enabling IPX networks to be connected across internets that carry only IP traffic.
sections.eli5: NetWare computers speak IPX, which doesn't work on the Internet. This method wraps IPX messages in UDP so they can cross the Internet.

sections.title: Packet Format and Checksum Handling
sections.content: Each IPX datagram is carried in the data portion of a UDP packet with all IP and UDP fields set normally. Both the source and destination ports in the UDP packet are set to UDP port 213, allocated by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority for IPX encapsulation. The transmitting party may avoid checksum overhead by setting the UDP checksum to zero, but UDP checksumming is highly recommended for IPX encapsulation since IPX implementations never use checksums themselves. The first two octets of every IPX header contain an IPX checksum field, but IPX packets are always sent with this set to all ones (FF hex), never zero. Implementations must ignore any UDP packets where the first two octets after the UDP header are not FF hex, as other values are reserved for future enhancements.
sections.eli5: The IPX message goes inside a UDP message aimed at port 213. Because IPX itself doesn't check for damage, the UDP layer's checksum is important to catch corruption.

sections.title: Address Mapping
sections.content: IPX addresses consist of a four-octet network number and a six-octet host number. The network number routes packets through the IPX internet to the destination network, while the six-octet host number identifies the specific host on that network. In this encapsulation scheme, the first two octets of the host number are always zero, and the last four octets are the node's four-octet IP address. This makes address mapping trivial: the encapsulation code extracts the last four octets of the IPX host number and uses that IP address as the destination address for the UDP/IP tunnel packet. This approach works because IPX routing information is exchanged in IPX headers, which means routers and end nodes learn the hardware addresses needed for forwarding packets.
sections.eli5: An IPX address has a network part and a host part. The host part is actually an IP address in disguise, so the code just pulls out the IP address and uses it.

sections.title: Broadcasting and Peer Networks
sections.content: IPX requires broadcast facilities for servers and routers to find one another. Since internet-wide IP broadcast is not available, IPX encapsulation uses a different approach: each server and router maintains a peer list of the IP addresses of all other IPX servers and routers on the IP internet. When IPX requests a broadcast, the encapsulation implementation simulates it by transmitting separate unicast packets to each peer. The peer list is constructed by hand, so multiple peer groups can share the same IP internet without knowing about each other, unlike a normal IPX network where all peers would auto-discover using hardware broadcast. The peer list could use IP multicast, but since multicast was not widely available when this RFC was written, no well-known multicast address was assigned. NetWare client nodes typically do not need to receive broadcasts, so they are not usually included in server peer lists, but clients must send broadcasts to locate servers and discover routes. A client implementation can handle this by having a configured list of IP addresses of all servers and routers, optionally including a broadcast address or multicast address when available.
sections.eli5: IPX normally broadcasts to find servers. On the Internet, that doesn't work, so administrators keep a list of server addresses and the client sends separate messages to each one.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit and Security
sections.content: The standard maximum transmission unit for IPX is 576 octets. With the 8-octet UDP header and 20-octet IP header, the resulting IP packets are 604 octets long, which exceeds the minimum 576 octets that all IP implementations are required to accept. Any IP implementation supporting IPX encapsulation must be capable of receiving 604-octet IP packets, and implementations should make the IPX maximum transmission unit configurable as protocols and hardware improve. Using an IP internet instead of physical cabling introduces security risks not normally encountered in isolated IPX networks. Physical media are typically protected from outside access, while IP internets invite outside access. The security of the entire IPX internetwork depends on the security of the entire IP internet through which it tunnels. Possible attacks include unauthorized IPX clients gaining access through password cracking, unauthorized IPX gateways diverting traffic to unintended routes, and unauthorized agents monitoring or manipulating IPX traffic on physical media controlled by them. IPX network administrators must be aware of these additional security risks.
sections.eli5: IPX packets are 576 bytes, but with IP and UDP headers they become 604 bytes. IPX tunneled through the Internet has the same security problems as any other Internet application, but Novell admins need to know about them.
